description: We chose the Flame in Freefall challenge because it is a unique and interesting topic that helps us understand how fire behaves in space without the normal effect of gravity. We wanted to explore the differences between fire on Earth and fire in microgravity.This challenge gives us an opportunity to learn about space science, combustion, and astronaut safety. We are also interested in understanding how scientific research can help prevent fire accidents in spacecraft and protect astronauts
summary:
**Project Summary – Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data**

Our project, *Flame in Freefall*, explores how flames behave in microgravity and how scientific data from space-based combustion experiments can improve fire safety on Earth and in space. We developed a concept for an SI-powered fire safety insight system that uses microgravity combustion data to understand flame behaviour, heat release, oxygen consumption and fire propagation under different conditions. By analysing these patterns, the project aims to identify potential fire hazards and support better fire detection, prevention and emergency response strategies. Unlike normal gravity, microgravity changes flame shape, airflow and combustion behaviour, making fire prediction more challenging, especially inside spacecraft. This project is important because it connects space research with real-world safety applications, helping engineers develop smarter fire protection systems, improve astronaut safety and contribute to safer buildings and enclosed environments on Earth.
details:
Project Details

Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data

1. Project Overview and Working Principle

Flame in Freefall is a space-science-based fire safety concept that explores how combustion behaves in microgravity and how this knowledge can improve fire safety in spacecraft and on Earth. The project focuses on understanding flame shape, flame propagation, heat release, oxygen availability and combustion behaviour under reduced-gravity conditions.

The proposed system follows a data-driven approach. It uses observations and measurements from microgravity combustion experiments to identify changes in flame behaviour. These observations can be compared with normal-gravity combustion patterns to understand the influence of gravity on fire development. The analysed information can then be translated into useful fire safety insights for monitoring, prevention and emergency response.

2. Benefits of the Project

  • Improves understanding of fire behaviour in microgravity environments.
  • Supports research into fire prevention and detection in spacecraft.
  • Helps identify the importance of oxygen availability and ventilation in combustion.
  • Provides insights that can contribute to safer enclosed environments.
  • Connects space research with practical civil engineering and safety applications.

3. Intended Impact

The main objective is to contribute to safer space missions by improving our understanding of combustion in spacecraft cabins. Fire incidents in enclosed space environments can be extremely dangerous because evacuation and firefighting options are limited.

The knowledge gained through this concept may also benefit buildings, laboratories, industrial facilities and other enclosed environments on Earth. Our long-term vision is to support the development of smarter fire detection, monitoring and prevention strategies.

4. Tools and Technologies

Our project is designed around scientific data interpretation and a conceptual engineering workflow.

  • NASA microgravity combustion research: Scientific background and experimental observations.
  • Microsoft PowerPoint: Presentation and visual explanation of the project.
  • Data analysis approach: Comparing flame characteristics and identifying combustion patterns.
  • Engineering concepts: Fire behaviour, oxygen supply, heat transfer, ventilation and fire safety principles.

Note: This is a conceptual data-analysis project. No physical fire detection hardware or fully operational software prototype has been developed.

5. Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of Flame in Freefall is its connection between space-based combustion research and real-world fire safety. Instead of considering fire behaviour only under normal gravitational conditions, our project focuses on the unusual flame patterns and combustion characteristics observed in microgravity.

It transforms complex scientific observations into understandable engineering insights that can support future fire safety solutions.

6. Factors Considered by Our Team

Our team considered:

  • Differences between normal gravity and microgravity.
  • Flame shape, size and propagation.
  • Oxygen availability and diffusion.
  • Heat transfer and combustion behaviour.
  • Ventilation and airflow in enclosed spaces.
  • Astronaut safety and emergency response limitations.
  • Practical applications of space research on Earth.
  • Scientific accuracy and the limitations of available experimental data.

7. Conclusion

Flame in Freefall demonstrates how understanding fire in space can contribute to safer environments both beyond Earth and on our planet. By connecting microgravity combustion observations with engineering-based fire safety insights, our project highlights the importance of scientific research, innovation and interdisciplinary thinking in solving real-world challenges.
